questions.stem: A 26-year-old male presented with diarrhea. He also had some blood in his stool, tenesmus, and a mucoid discharge from his anus. He had had unprotected receptive anal intercourse 1 week earlier. Investigations: 4th generation HIV Ag/Ab negative Syphilis EIA negative Urine NAAT for gonorrhea and chlamydia negative Rectal NAAT testing positive for C. trachomatis, negative for N. gonorrhoeae
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Benzathine penicillin G for one dose
Cefixime orally in a single dose
Doxycycline for 7 days plus one dose of azithromycin

questions.explanation: Doxycycline for 21 days LGV can result in proctitis and proctocolitis. This may manifest as tenesmus, rectal bleeding, and mucoid discharge from the rectum. Laboratory diagnostics to distinguish LGV serovars of C. trachomatis are not widely available. The patient should be treated for LGV based upon the clinical presentation and positive C. trachomatis by NAAT . Treatment course for LGV proctitis is doxycycline 100 mg BD for 21 days.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q11

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman presented for antenatal care at 6/40 weeks pregnant. She was sexually active, with 5 casual male partners in the last year. Investigations: 4th generation HIV Ag/Ab negative Syphilis EIA negative Vaginal swab NAAT negative for Neisseria gonorrhoeae, positive for Chlamydia trachomatis One gram of azithromycin was administered orally for one dose.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Give a stat dose of ceftriaxone IM
Give an additional 1 gram of azithromycin in 4 weeks
Give weekly suppressive azithromycin 1 gram until delivery
Repeat Chlamydia NAAT at 36/40 or before delivery
Repeat Chlamydia NAAT in 4 weeks for test of cure

questions.explanation: Repeat Chlamydia NAAT in 4 weeks for test of cure Test of cure for Chlamydia is recommended during pregnancy. This recommendation was put in place to prevent the severe sequelae that can occur in mothers and neonates if infection persists. Repeat screening in the 3rd trimester may be warranted based upon patient risk. However, it is not the best of the options.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q10

questions.stem: A 23-year-old man presented to the HIV clinic complaining of painful swellings in his groin. On examination he has no genital ulcers or chancres, but he has large bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy. You suspect he has a sexually transmitted disease.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Lymphogranuloma venereum. questions.question: 6. Regarding LGV

parts.text: What is the specific pathogen?
What are two manifestations of secondary LGV (note, you cannot name the same manifestation at two different body sites)
What are two screening tests for LGV that are available in typical clinical situations
What is one confirmatory test that can be done

cohort_answer.text: Pathogen: Serotype L1, L2, or L3 of Chlamydia trachomatis. Secondary LGV manifestations: direct extension to lymph nodes/inguinal syndrome of painful lymph nodes; proctitis. Screening tests: NAAT of lesions/specimens; serology (low sensitivity early). Confirmatory test: culture, genotyping

questions.question: LGV

parts.text: Name, genus, serovars
What is the specific test to diagnose LGV?
What is the first line treatment (dose and duration)?

cohort_answer.text: Lymphogranuloma venereum; Chlamydia trachomatis; serovars L1, L2, L3. Diagnostic test: NAAT testing; serovar-specific confirmatory testing using DNA sequencing or RFLP; PCR-based genotyping (not widely available); Chlamydia serology (complement fixation titers >1:64 or microimmunofluorescence titers >1:256) may support diagnosis. Treatment: Doxycycline 100mg PO BID x21 days.

questions.question: LGV

parts.text: What causes LGV (genus and species), and list the three serotypes?
What is the confirmatory test specific for LGV?
What is the treatment for LGV? (Drug, route, dose, duration)

questions.model_answer:
a) Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, specifically serovars (genotypes) L1, L2, and L3.
b) Confirmatory test specific for LGV: molecular genotyping (an LGV-specific PCR/NAAT targeting the L1, L2, or L3 serovar-specific gene, such as the ompA gene), since standard commercial NAATs cannot distinguish LGV from non-LGV C. trachomatis serovars.
c) Treatment: Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 21 days (erythromycin is an alternative if doxycycline cannot be used).

questions.question: Regarding lymphogranuloma venereum:

parts.text: What is the specific organism associated with this infection.
List TWO manifestations of secondary lymphogranuloma venereum.
List TWO screening laboratory tests that can be performed that suggest this infection.
List ONE laboratory test that can be performed to confirm this infection.

questions.model_answer:
a) Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, specifically serovars (genotypes) L1, L2, and L3.
b) Two manifestations of secondary-stage LGV: (1) painful, tender inguinal and/or femoral lymphadenopathy (bubo formation, sometimes with the "groove sign"), and (2) LGV proctocolitis (mucopurulent anal discharge, tenesmus, and rectal bleeding), particularly seen in MSM.
c) Screening tests suggesting LGV: a standard Chlamydia trachomatis NAAT (nucleic acid amplification test) positive result (though it cannot distinguish LGV from non-LGV serovars) and complement fixation serology showing an elevated/rising antibody titer (suggestive given the higher titers seen with the more invasive LGV disease).
d) Confirmatory test specific for LGV: molecular genotyping (an LGV-specific PCR/NAAT targeting the L1, L2, or L3 serovar-specific gene, such as the ompA gene), since standard commercial NAATs cannot distinguish LGV from non-LGV C. trachomatis serovars.

parts.text: What is the organism that causes LGV?
What are two clinical presentations of infection?
What is one screening test for this?
What is one confirmatory test for this?

questions.model_answer:
a) Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, specifically serovars (genotypes) L1, L2, and L3.
b) Two manifestations of secondary-stage LGV: (1) painful, tender inguinal and/or femoral lymphadenopathy (bubo formation, sometimes with the "groove sign"), and (2) LGV proctocolitis (mucopurulent anal discharge, tenesmus, and rectal bleeding), particularly seen in MSM.
c) Screening test: Chlamydia trachomatis NAAT (positive, though it cannot distinguish LGV from non-LGV serovars).
d) Confirmatory test: LGV-specific genotyping/PCR (or complement fixation serology with a high/rising titer).

questions.question: Preferred therapy

parts.text: B) Chlamydia cervicitis in pregnancy

cohort_answer.text: Amoxicillin 500mg PO tid x7 days OR Azithromycin 1g PO x1; Erythromycin 2g/day PO in divided doses for 7 days. Treatment same for urethral, cervical, rectal chlamydia. Do not use doxy or FQ in pregnancy. If using alternative to 1st line therapy must do test of cure 3-4 weeks after treatment (needed only if using amox or erythromycin)

questions.question: Pregnant woman with untreated Chlamydia presents at delivery. Hx of anaphylaxis to macrolides in the past

parts.text: How to manage mom and baby?
Rationale for treating baby?

cohort_answer.text: A) Mom: allergic to azithro, no doxy or FQ in pregnancy/lactation; Amoxicillin 500mg PO TID x7 days (similar efficacy to azithro); test of cure 3-4 weeks after tx complete in all pregnant women when using penicillin; also test for gonorrhea, syphilis, HIV at delivery, notify public health. Baby: close follow up monitoring for neonatal chlamydia (conjunctivitis, pneumonia); if develop sx, swab conjunctiva or NP and tx if positive. B) Minimize complications of neonatal inclusion conjunctivitis (cause of ophthalmia neonatorum) or neonatal pneumonia.

parts.text: Bacteria genus + species, and serovars
How to make specific diagnosis
Treatment, dose, duration

cohort_answer.text: Bacteria/serovars: Chlamydia trachomatis serovars 1, 2, 3. Diagnosis: PCR based genotyping from genital/rectal swab or serology. Treatment: Doxycycline 100mg PO BID x 3/52

questions.question: A 17F female presents to the hospital. She recently delivered and did not have any prenatal care. Her baby has purulent conjunctivitis and a cough.

parts.text: What is the most likely diagnosis?
What are 3 tests you would order?
What is the treatment for baby?
What treatment would you give the mother?

cohort_answer.text: Diagnosis: Ophthalmia neonatorum, Gonococcal vs Chlamydia conjunctivitis (chlamydia more common). Tests: Conjunctival swab for culture/gram stain (gonococcal, chlamydia); throat swab for culture/gram stain; throat swab for NAAT (chlamydia and gonorrhea). Baby treatment: CRO/CTX IM x1 (ceftriaxone preferred unless significant hyperbilirubinemia) for gonococcal disease; erythromycin x14 days for chlamydia pneumonia (given cough). Mother treatment: CRO 250mg IM x1 + azithromycin x1 (treats gonorrhea given high concomitant chlamydia rates); in high risk cases (no prenatal care, substance use, hx STIs) can treat pre-emptively while awaiting micro results.

questions.question: AM 17. STI in MSM - list non-viral causes to species level of urethritis with the treatment including dose and route according to PHAC (4)

parts.text: List non-viral causes with treatment for N. gonorrhoeae, C. trachomatis, Mycoplasma genitalium, Mycoplasma hominis, Ureaplasma urealyticum, Trichomonas vaginalis

cohort_answer.text: N. gonorrhoeae - ceftriaxone 250mg IM + 1g Azithromycin. C. trachomatis - azithromycin 1g PO or doxy 100mg PO BID x7d. Trichomonas vaginalis - metronidazole 2g x1 or 500mg PO BID x7d. Mycoplasma genitalium - Azithromycin 500mg x1 then 250mg PO x2-5d (if previously treated with azithro, Moxi 400mg daily x7d; if PID, Moxi 400 x14d); NAAT is diagnostic test of choice, routine screening not recommended. Ureaplasma urealyticum - doxycycline 100mg PO BID x7 days (no PHAC guideline; Sanford: doxy or azithro 1g x1).

questions.question: Neonatal conjunctivitis differential based on timing/presentation.

parts.text: Bilateral/rapid onset/purulent presentation, usually pus wipes out and comes right back - what is this?
Unilateral or bilateral, usually 5 to 14 days after delivery - what is this?
Diagnostic test

cohort_answer.text: Rapid bilateral purulent conjunctivitis (pus recurs immediately after wiping) = gonococcal conjunctivitis. Onset 5-14 days after delivery = C. trachomatis inclusion conjunctivitis. Diagnosis is clinical, confirmed by lab testing: Gram stain and culture (chocolate agar and Thayer-Martin media for gonorrhea, blood agar for other organisms); Giemsa stain for chlamydial suspicion, though NAAT now more commonly used (less expensive, less labor than viral culture). Newborns with suspected C. trachomatis infection should have samples drawn from both conjunctivae and oropharynx; swabs should include conjunctival epithelial cells since C. trachomatis is an obligate intracellular organism.

questions.question: Purulent conjunctivitis in a neonate whose mother is street involved.

parts.text: What are 3 samples to send for diagnosis and to identify potential complications?
What are 3 other neonatal sites of infection to be concerned about?
What agent to treat a neonate with?
What are two regimens to treat mother with?

questions.model_answer: a) Three samples for diagnosis/complications: (1) Conjunctival swab for Gram stain and culture (chocolate/Thayer-Martin media) plus NAAT for N. gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis. (2) Blood culture (assess for disseminated gonococcal infection/sepsis). (3) CSF analysis/culture if signs of sepsis or meningitis present. b) Three other neonatal sites of concern: disseminated infection/bacteremia, septic arthritis, and scalp abscess (from fetal monitor electrode site); rhinitis also acceptable. c) Neonatal treatment: ceftriaxone 25-50 mg/kg IV/IM single dose (max 250 mg), with saline eye irrigation. d) Two maternal treatment regimens: (1) Ceftriaxone 250 mg IM single dose (gonorrhea) plus azithromycin 1 g PO single dose (chlamydia coverage). (2) If cephalosporin-allergic, azithromycin 2 g PO single dose (alternative gonorrhea regimen).

questions.question: Neonate with bilateral purulent conjunctivitis 3d after birth. Mom has RF for STI.

parts.text: Name causative pathogen genus and spp
Diagnosis (2-3 tests)
Therapy

questions.model_answer: a) Causative pathogen (genus/species): Neisseria gonorrhoeae (hyperacute purulent conjunctivitis presenting within the first few days of life is classic for gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum, versus chlamydial which typically presents 5-14 days after birth). b) Diagnosis (2-3 tests): Gram stain of conjunctival exudate (intracellular gram-negative diplococci), culture on chocolate/Thayer-Martin selective media, and NAAT for N. gonorrhoeae (and co-testing for C. trachomatis). c) Therapy: ceftriaxone 25-50 mg/kg IV/IM single dose (max 250 mg) with saline eye irrigation; treat mother (and partner) empirically as well.

questions.question: A baby is born to a young mother who is living on the street, and who abandons her child in hospital so no further history is available. The baby develops bilateral purulent conjunctivitis.

parts.text: What is the most likely causative organism, to the genus and species?
What are three other neonatal manifestations of infection with this organism?
What are three microbiologic investigations that you would like to do for the baby?
What would be your recommended treatment, assuming that conjunctivitis is the only site involved?
What 2 empiric treatments would you recommend for the mother, if she returns?

questions.model_answer: a) Most likely organism: Neisseria gonorrhoeae. b) Other neonatal manifestations (3): disseminated infection/bacteremia, septic arthritis, scalp abscess (also rhinitis, sepsis). c) Microbiologic investigations (3): Gram stain of eye discharge, culture on chocolate/Thayer-Martin selective media, blood culture to assess for dissemination. d) Treatment if conjunctivitis only: ceftriaxone 25-50 mg/kg IV/IM single dose (max 250 mg) with saline irrigation. e) Empiric maternal treatment (2 drugs): ceftriaxone 250 mg IM x1 plus azithromycin 1 g PO x1.

parts.text: List 3 causes of genital ulcers in which Doxycycline can be used as a treatment

cohort_answer.text: Syphilis; Chlamydia trachomatis (serovars L1, L2, L3) - lymphogranuloma venereum, first line rx is doxy x21 days; Klebsiella granulomatis (donovanosis/granuloma inguinale): first line is azithro +/- gent, but doxy or Septra x3 wks are alternative regimens

questions.question: Name the first-line treatment regimen for the following infections in men who have sex with men, as per the Public Health Agency of Canada.

parts.text: Neisseria gonorrhoea
Chlamydia trachomatis
Mycoplasma genitalium
Trichomonas vaginalis
Ureaplasma urealyticum

questions.model_answer: PHAC first-line MSM STI regimens: (1) N. gonorrhoeae - ceftriaxone 250 mg IM single dose plus azithromycin 1 g PO single dose (dual therapy, especially given pharyngeal involvement common in MSM). (2) C. trachomatis - doxycycline 100 mg PO BID x7 days (preferred over azithromycin for rectal chlamydia, common in MSM). (3) Mycoplasma genitalium - doxycycline 100 mg PO BID x7 days followed by azithromycin 1 g PO then 500 mg daily x3 days (if macrolide-susceptible), or moxifloxacin 400 mg daily x7-14 days if resistance/failure. (4) Trichomonas vaginalis - metronidazole 2 g PO single dose. (5) Ureaplasma urealyticum - doxycycline 100 mg PO BID x7 days.

questions.question: 27-year old man with chlamydia, gonorrhea and treponemal test positive. His RPR is 1:256, w (NOTE: did not specify location of Chlamydia/gonorrhea infection, or whether patient is MSM etc) per PHAC

parts.text: What 3 drugs would you treat with? Include dose, route, duration
What are 2 reasons for RPR not decreasing 4 fold at 12 months, other than incorrect clinical staging at diagnosis

questions.model_answer:
a) 3 drugs with dose/route/duration: (1) benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM x1 dose for syphilis (assuming early syphilis given the high titer); (2) ceftriaxone 250 mg IM x1 dose for gonorrhea; (3) doxycycline 100 mg PO BID x7 days for chlamydia.
b) 2 reasons RPR fails to decline 4-fold by 12 months (other than incorrect staging): (1) HIV coinfection, which can blunt/delay the serologic response to treatment; (2) reinfection with a new syphilis exposure during the follow-up period.

questions.question: Q69 (2023 Day 1). 27 year old male with RPR 1:128 (negative RPR 3 months ago), positive chlamydia and gonorrhea. No specific symptoms mentioned. (HIV/STI)

parts.text: List 3 antibiotics indicated including name, dose, route, and frequency
If RPR not 4 fold decrease give 2 reasons why

cohort_answer.text:
Syphilis: Early (Primary, Secondary, early latent) - Benzathine Penicillin G 2.4 million units IM x1. Late (Late latent, tertiary) - Benzathine Penicillin G 2.4 million units IM weekly x3. Neurosyphilis - Crystalline Pen G 4 million units q4h IV x14 days.
Chlamydia: Doxycycline 100mg PO BID x7 days.
Gonorrhea: Ceftriaxone 250mg IM x1.
If RPR not 4-fold decrease, 2 reasons: Recurrent infection; Neurosyphilis; Inadequate treatment.

questions.question: You are assessing a 1-day old infant born to a mother with untreated Chlamydia trachomatis infection.

parts.text: What prophylaxis or antiviral therapy, if any, does the infant require?
What are two classical clinical presentations of this infection that could present within a few weeks?
If the baby needs treatment, name the class of antimicrobial therapy you would use?

questions.model_answer:
a) No specific antibiotic prophylaxis is recommended for an asymptomatic infant born to a mother with untreated chlamydial infection; routine neonatal ocular erythromycin prophylaxis (given for gonococcal ophthalmia prevention) does not reliably prevent chlamydial conjunctivitis or pneumonia. The infant should instead be closely monitored clinically for signs of infection and treated if they develop.
b) Two classical presentations that can occur within the first weeks of life: (1) neonatal (inclusion) conjunctivitis, typically presenting 5-14 days after birth. (2) Infant (afebrile) pneumonia syndrome, typically presenting between 4 and 12 weeks of age with staccato cough and tachypnea.
c) If treatment is needed, the antimicrobial class of choice is a macrolide (e.g., oral erythromycin or azithromycin).

questions.question: List of various STIs - what investigations (if any) are indicated, and first line tx option for each?

parts.text: B) MSM with painful LAD

cohort_answer.text: Consider LGV (Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1, L2, L3). Request special testing for LGV from urine (+/- rectal, throat) +/- LN aspiration. Treatment: doxy or azithro x21 days

questions.question: Preferred treatments: Chlamydia cervicitis in pregnancy; Group B strep ppx

parts.text: Chlamydia cervicitis in pregnancy
Group B strep ppx

cohort_answer.text: Chlamydia cervicitis in pregnancy: Azithromycin 1g PO x1 dose. Group B strep ppx: IV PenG 5mU or Ampicillin 2g IV or Cefazolin 2g IV at least 4h before birth. Risk factors for neonatal GBS sepsis: maternal colonization during current pregnancy, GBS bacteriuria, prior infant with invasive GBS disease, prolonged rupture of membranes, maternal fever. For colonization, risk of sepsis is 1-2%. Screen women at 35-37 weeks GA.

questions.question: Based on PHAC guidelines, name the recommended first-line treatment for the following for the MSM community (drug, dose, route, duration).

parts.text: Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Chlamydia trachomatis
Trichomonas vaginalis
Mycoplasma genitalium
Ureaplasma urealyticum

cohort_answer.text: Neisseria gonorrhoeae: Ceftriaxone 250mg IM once PLUS Azithromycin 1g PO once. Chlamydia trachomatis: Doxycycline 100mg PO bid x7 days (for LGV treat 21d). Trichomonas vaginalis: Metronidazole 2g PO once. Mycoplasma genitalium: Azithromycin 500mg PO day 1 followed by 250mg PO for total of 5d. Ureaplasma urealyticum: Doxycycline 100mg PO bid x7 days
